Numismatic Report: The 1944 Lincoln Cent, commonly known as a Wheat Penny, is significant for being struck during World War II. After the experimental 1943 steel cents (due to copper shortages for wartime munitions), the U.S. Mint returned to a brass alloy (95% copper, 5% zinc/tin) for cents in 1944. This composition was largely derived from reclaimed shell casings, making these coins a tangible piece of American wartime recycling efforts. Millions were minted at Philadelphia, Denver, and San Francisco, making them very common in circulated grades. The 'Wheat Ears' reverse design, introduced in 1909, remained until 1958.
